planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest, or in late summer for a fall crop; Pablo is a dark red romaine hybrid grown for its uniform, upright heads and slower bolting than many older red romaine varieties.

directions: Sow seed shallowly and keep the bed consistently moist for even germination, then thin seedlings to their final spacing once true leaves appear. Pablo is a dark burgundy-red romaine hybrid that holds its rich color and upright, well-filled head shape more reliably than many open-pollinated red romaines, with a crisp texture and mild flavor typical of romaine types. It tolerates a bit more heat before bolting than many red lettuces, giving it a somewhat longer productive window into late spring, though it still performs best in the cool shoulder seasons in a Gulf Coast garden. Harvest whole heads once fully formed, or pull individual outer leaves for a cut-and-come-again harvest over several weeks, and provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture to further delay bolting as temperatures rise.

common_name: Cincinnati Market Radish (Long Red Heirloom Radish)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or again in late summer for a fall crop; Cincinnati Market is a nineteenth-century heirloom producing long, slender, bright red roots with crisp, mild white flesh.

directions: Sow seed a half-inch deep directly in loose, well-worked soil, and thin seedlings early to a couple of inches apart so roots have room to elongate without forking. Cincinnati Market is an old market-garden heirloom prized for its long, cylindrical, bright scarlet-red roots with crisp, mild-flavored white flesh that stays tender without turning pithy or overly hot if harvested promptly at full size. It matures quickly, making it a reliable choice for succession sowing every couple of weeks through the cool season for a steady radish supply, and its uniform, attractive shape made it a historic favorite for market bunching. Keep the soil consistently moist as roots size up, since inconsistent watering causes cracking and harsh flavor, and harvest promptly once roots reach full size, since radishes left too long in warm soil quickly turn woody and overly pungent.

common_name: Lunar White Carrot (Pale Ivory Sweet Carrot)

planting.note: Direct sow into deeply worked, loose, stone-free soil in early spring or late summer; Lunar White is a pigment-free white carrot grown for its mild, sweet flavor and striking appearance in mixed rainbow carrot bunches.

directions: Sow seed thinly and shallowly in deeply worked, loose, sandy loam free of rocks and clumps, keeping the surface consistently moist until the slow-germinating seedlings emerge. Lunar White produces smooth, tapered, ivory-white roots with a crisp texture and mild, sweet flavor free of the slight bitterness some white carrots carry, making it a popular addition to mixed-color carrot bunches for market and home use. Because it lacks the orange and purple pigments of most carrots, it shows soil staining and surface blemishes more readily, so grow it in well-worked, debris-free soil for the cleanest roots. Thin seedlings early to prevent crowded, twisted roots, keep beds weeded while carrots are young and slow to establish, and harvest once roots reach full size, since white carrots left too long in the ground can develop a coarser texture.

planting.note: Start indoors 3-4 weeks before the last frost or direct sow once soil is warm; Mexican Sour Gherkin is a Central American vine related to cucumbers that produces hundreds of tiny, grape-sized fruit that look like miniature watermelons and taste like tangy, sour cucumbers.

directions: Transplant or direct sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and provide a trellis or fence for the thin, wiry, climbing vines, which are more delicate looking than standard cucumber vines but grow just as vigorously in heat. Mexican Sour Gherkin, also called cucamelon or mouse melon, is a distinct species related to cucumbers, native to Mexico and Central America, that produces an enormous number of grape-to-thumb-sized fruit with the striped look of a tiny watermelon and a crisp, tangy, cucumber-with-a-citrusy-sour-edge flavor, eaten whole, skin and all. The heat-loving vines shrug off the humid Gulf Coast summer far better than standard cucumbers and keep producing steadily through conditions that stall out most other cucurbits, with harvest starting once fruits reach about an inch long and firm. Pick regularly, since the tiny fruits go from perfect to overripe quickly, and the vigorous vines benefit from vertical support both to save space and to keep the abundant fruit clean and easy to spot.
